batch_note: Yes, in three ways. (1) Key-letter sequences repeat across sub-cohorts: A-01..06 and D-01..06 are both C,A,D,B,D,A, and B-01..06 is C,A,D,B,C,A. The overall letter spread is 6/6/6/6, so a per-cohort histogram will not catch it. Shuffle within each sub-cohort independently. (2) All 12 hypothesis items use one 2x2 template: the key is always the comparison that changes only one factor, and the both-vs-neither option is never keyed. A student who learns that the confounded comparison is never right strikes one option per item for free. Each remaining item still needs the matrix built, so this is a weak tell, not a fatal one. (3) Table items: in II22A-06, II22C-06 and II22B-06 the key is the only comparison that breaks the trend, and the other options show the ordinary pattern on sight. II22A-06 and II22C-06 share the same phrasing: the lower or nearer site is named first with the larger value. II22D-04's distractors share one identical ratio. All 24 keys matched my cold answers and none is defective, so I recommend no drops. The fixes are re-shuffling the letters and varying the trend-reversal items' distractors.

II22A-01.note2: Key C is the only noise-against comparison; explanation correctly classes A and D as supporting and B as confounded.

II22A-02.note2: Cassel vs Fairlie isolates fungi; the explanation's handling of the shade comparisons is sound.

II22A-03.note2: Bypass earlier than the lit quiet lanes is the one comparison against lamps; the reasoning holds.

II22A-05.note2: Carrow Point 35/64 is the only colony above half; sound, but easy for a hard-route slot.

II22A-06.note2: Key correct, but the key is the only option naming the lower site first with the larger value, and B and C are on-trend increases struck on sight; this phrasing tell, shared with II22C-06, is worth fixing.

II22B-01.note2: North July over north March weakens freeze-thaw; correct, though it is the lone option favouring a non-freeze-thaw window.
